papers.what_it_is: A learning-theory paper that introduces mixture-of-superpositions quantum examples, gives quantum algorithms for distributional agnostic learning of parities and Fourier-sparse functions under uniform input marginal, proves a classical verifier can check such learning under promises on the distribution, and proves distribution-independent sample-complexity lower bounds.

The formal results (Theorems 7 to 16) hold only under promises: the distribution must lie in a class with no small non-zero Fourier coefficients (and, for the distributional case, a bounded squared l2 norm of the label expectation), the accuracy has a lower limit that depends on that bias gap, parities are verified 1-agnostically but Fourier-sparse functions only 2-agnostically and improperly, and the verifier has an accuracy floor that cannot be improved without a verifier cost linear in the input length (Theorem 13). Section 6.1 says the verification protocols need an additional assumption beyond the learning algorithms.
existing.value: The authors state that the verification results need an additional assumption on the unknown function or distribution (a class with no small non-zero Fourier coefficients, with a bounded squared norm of the label expectation in the distributional case), and prove verification of agnostic parity learning (proper) and Fourier-sparse learning (improper, with agnostic factor of two) by a classical verifier with random-example or statistical-query access; the separation is unconditional for statistical-query access and conditional on the hardness of Learning Parity with Noise for random-example access.

papers.title_in_file: Solving various NP-Hard problems using exponentially fewer qubits on a Quantum Computer
papers.version_note: arXiv 2301.06978v2, 12 Jan 2024 (dated 15 January 2024 on the first page). The text layer holds the paper twice (two layouts); the first copy was read and the second used to check quotes. Several tables (Table IV, V, VI, and the Table I solution columns) came out partly or fully without their numbers, and figures 3 to 6 are plots; the captions and surrounding text were read.
papers.what_it_is: A hybrid variational method that encodes a Maximum Cut instance of n nodes in ceil(log2 n) qubits (after Rancic), extended by reductions and a QUBO reformulation to other NP-hard problems, tested on a simulator up to 128 nodes and on IBM devices up to 256 nodes.

existing.note: The count |V| − 1 is given without derivation, and the comparison with p|E| relies on the authors' statement that it is easy to see p|E| ≫ |V| at higher densities, with p ≫ 1 for practical purposes. No transpiled gate counts after hardware mapping are reported.
existing.certainty_reason: Low: as the paper reports it.

existing.note: The log-qubit encoding is from Rančić (reference 26); this paper builds on it. The sentence is a statement of a cited result, not a new one.
existing.certainty_reason: Low: as the paper reports it.

existing.note: Also: the QPU times in Table VI exclude queue time; the stated real-world time of hours or days is the reason larger instances were not run.
existing.certainty_reason: Low: as the paper reports it.

existing.note: The 'nearly or over 90% of the optimal cut' sentence is made for the 64-node instances, where the ILP optimum (to a 4% integrality gap) is the benchmark. For 128 and 256 nodes the ILP did not converge in 2 days, so the benchmark is the Goemans-Williamson (GW) range, and QPU results there are 82.5 to 92.8 percent of the GW range. The QPU run on 32 nodes is 83.58 percent of optimal.
existing.value: The authors report that for the 64-node Maximum Cut instances all results are nearly or over 90% of the optimal cut found by an ILP solver, that for 128 and 256 nodes the ILP did not converge in more than 2 days so the Goemans Williamson method was used for benchmarking, and that a real quantum computer was used for instances up to 256 nodes.

assertions.value: The paper gives reductions of Minimum Partition, Maximum 2-Sat and (via 2-Sat) Maximum Clique to Maximum Cut; Minimum Partition uses an edge of weight wi times wj for every pair, an n-variable Maximum 2-Sat becomes a 2n-node Maximum Cut, an n-node Maximum Clique becomes a 2(n + 1)-node Maximum Cut, and the authors note the conversions may not scale one to one.

It will require ⌈log2 2n⌉ = (1 + ⌈log2 n⌉) qubits, or, in other words, 1 more qubit than the original algorithm.
